name: kubectl
description: Protects against destructive kubectl operations like delete namespace, \ drain, and mass deletion

destructive_patterns.name: delete-namespace
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete namespace removes the entire namespace and ALL resources within it.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a namespace destroys EVERYTHING inside it:

\ - All deployments, pods, services \ - All configmaps and secrets \ - All persistent volume claims (data may be lost) \ - All ingresses and network policies \ - All RBAC resources scoped to the namespace

\ This is irreversible. Even if you recreate the namespace, all resources are gone.

\ Preview what would be deleted: \ kubectl get all -n <namespace> \ kubectl get pvc -n <namespace>

\ Safer approach: \ kubectl delete deployment <name> -n <namespace> # Delete specific resources

destructive_patterns.name: delete-all
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete --all removes ALL resources of that type. Use --dry-run=client first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
The --all flag deletes EVERY resource of the specified type in the namespace.

\ For example: \ - kubectl delete pods --all: Kills all pods (services go down) \ - kubectl delete svc --all: Removes all services (networking breaks) \ - kubectl delete pvc --all: May delete all persistent data

\ Always preview first: \ kubectl delete <resource> --all --dry-run=client

\ Safer alternative: \ kubectl delete <resource> -l app=myapp # Use label selectors

destructive_patterns.name: delete-all-namespaces
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete with -A/--all-namespaces affects ALL namespaces. Very dangerous!
destructive_patterns.explanation:
The -A/--all-namespaces flag expands deletion to EVERY namespace in the cluster. \ This can take down your entire cluster:

\ - Production, staging, and dev environments affected \ - System namespaces (kube-system) may be impacted \ - Cross-namespace resources and dependencies break

\ This is almost never what you want. Always specify a namespace: \ kubectl delete <resource> -n <namespace>

\ Preview cluster-wide resources: \ kubectl get <resource> -A

destructive_patterns.name: drain-node
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl drain evicts all pods from a node. Ensure proper pod disruption budgets.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
kubectl drain evicts ALL pods from a node, typically for maintenance. \ This can cause service disruption:

\ - All pods are evicted (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets) \ - DaemonSet pods remain unless --ignore-daemonsets is used \ - Pods with local storage fail unless --delete-emptydir-data is used \ - Without replicas elsewhere, services go down

\ Before draining: \ kubectl get pods -o wide | grep <node> # Check what's running \ kubectl get pdb -A # Check disruption budgets

\ Safer approach: \ kubectl cordon <node> # Prevent new pods first, then drain gradually

destructive_patterns.name: cordon-node
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl cordon marks a node unschedulable. Existing pods continue running.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
kubectl cordon marks a node as unschedulable. Existing pods continue running, \ but no new pods will be scheduled to this node.

\ Use cases: \ - Preparing for maintenance \ - Investigating node issues \ - Gradual migration

\ To reverse: \ kubectl uncordon <node>

\ Check node status: \ kubectl get nodes \ kubectl describe node <node> | grep Taints

destructive_patterns.name: taint-noexecute
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl taint with NoExecute evicts existing pods that don't tolerate the taint.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
A NoExecute taint immediately evicts pods that don't have a matching toleration. \ This is more aggressive than NoSchedule:

\ - Existing pods are evicted (not just new scheduling blocked) \ - Can cause immediate service disruption \ - Pods may not have time for graceful shutdown

\ Check current taints: \ kubectl describe node <node> | grep Taints

\ Consider NoSchedule first: \ kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:NoSchedule

\ Remove taint: \ kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:NoExecute-

destructive_patterns.name: delete-workload
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete deployment/statefulset/daemonset removes the workload. Use --dry-run first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a workload terminates all its pods:

\ - Deployment: All replicas terminated, service goes down \ - StatefulSet: Ordered shutdown, PVCs may be orphaned \ - DaemonSet: Removed from all nodes \ - ReplicaSet: Pods terminated (usually managed by Deployment)

\ Preview first: \ kubectl delete <type> <name> --dry-run=client \ kubectl get pods -l app=<name> # Check affected pods

\ Consider scaling down first: \ kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=0

destructive_patterns.name: delete-pvc
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete pvc may permanently delete data if ReclaimPolicy is Delete.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a PVC can cause permanent data loss depending on the PV's reclaimPolicy:

\ - Delete: Underlying storage is deleted (DATA LOST) \ - Retain: PV is kept but becomes 'Released' (manual recovery needed) \ - Recycle: Deprecated, data scrubbed

\ Check the reclaim policy: \ kubectl get pv <pv-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy}'

\ Backup first: \ kubectl exec <pod> -- tar czf - /data > backup.tar.gz

\ Preview: \ kubectl delete pvc <name> --dry-run=client

destructive_patterns.name: delete-pv
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete pv may permanently delete the underlying storage.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a PersistentVolume can permanently destroy the underlying storage:

\ - Cloud disks (EBS, GCE PD, Azure Disk) may be deleted \ - NFS mounts become orphaned \ - Local storage data is lost

\ Even with Retain policy, deleting the PV may trigger storage cleanup.

\ Check what's using the PV: \ kubectl get pvc -A | grep <pv-name>

\ Check storage class policy: \ kubectl get storageclass <class> -o yaml

\ Preview: \ kubectl delete pv <name> --dry-run=client

destructive_patterns.name: scale-to-zero
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl scale --replicas=0 stops all pods for the workload.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Scaling to zero replicas terminates ALL pods for the workload:

\ - Service becomes unavailable \ - Endpoints are removed from Service \ - In-flight requests are dropped \ - StatefulSets: Ordered shutdown from highest ordinal

\ This is often intentional but can cause outages if done accidentally.

\ Check current replicas: \ kubectl get deployment <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'

\ To restore: \ kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=<N>

destructive_patterns.name: delete-force
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete --force --grace-period=0 immediately removes resources without graceful shutdown.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Force deletion with zero grace period is dangerous:

\ - Pods are killed immediately (no SIGTERM, just gone) \ - In-flight requests fail \ - Data corruption risk if writes in progress \ - Finalizers may be skipped (resource leak)

\ Kubernetes warns against this. Use only for stuck pods that won't terminate.

\ Try graceful deletion first: \ kubectl delete pod <name> # Default 30s grace \ kubectl delete pod <name> --grace-period=60 # Extended grace

\ Check why pod is stuck: \ kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 Status

destructive_patterns.name: apply-force
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl apply --force deletes and recreates resources, causing downtime.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
kubectl apply --force deletes the resource and recreates it from the manifest. \ This causes:

\ - Downtime as pods are terminated before new ones start \ - Loss of any runtime modifications \ - Potential data loss for stateful workloads \ - Disruption to in-flight requests

\ Use this only when you cannot update resources normally due to immutable field changes.

\ Preview changes first: \ kubectl diff -f <file>

\ Try server-side apply for safer updates: \ kubectl apply --server-side -f <file>

destructive_patterns.name: delete-from-stdin
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete -f - deletes every resource described by stdin without a reviewable manifest path.
destructive_patterns.explanation: Materialize the manifest, inspect it with kubectl diff, and run kubectl delete --dry-run=client before deleting the resources.

destructive_patterns.name: delete-from-directory
destructive_patterns.description: kubectl delete -f with directories or --recursive deletes many resources at once.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting from a directory or recursively removes ALL resources defined in those files:

\ - Multiple deployments, services, configmaps deleted at once \ - Hard to recover if wrong directory \ - No confirmation or preview by default

\ Always preview first: \ kubectl diff -f <directory> \ ls -la <directory>/*.yaml

\ Delete specific files instead: \ kubectl delete -f <specific-file.yaml>
